topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings based on employer perspectives on AI literacy and curriculum needs, but geographic scope and sample size not evident from title/snippet alone. Generalisability may be limited by which employers were surveyed and their industry representation.
takeaways: Identify the specific AI literacy competencies your organisation's roles require by consulting with department leaders and job-level stakeholders — don't assume one-size-fits-all training.
Use employer feedback on curriculum priorities to design targeted upskilling programmes that address actual workforce gaps rather than generic AI awareness modules.
Assess current employee AI readiness levels through skills audits before rolling out literacy initiatives to ensure training meets your team where they are.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; competency frameworks may not fully transfer to other regions with different health systems, regulatory environments, or digital infrastructure maturity.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are most critical for your public health workforce (e.g., data literacy, digital tool proficiency, cybersecurity awareness) and prioritise upskilling in those areas first rather than attempting comprehensive training.
Use the framework to benchmark your organisation's current capability gaps against established European standards, then design targeted capability-building programmes for different roles.
Ensure competency development includes both technical skills and change management capabilities, as adoption of digital tools requires staff to understand not just how to use them, but why and when.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workforce AI literacy development would require adaptation of pedagogical frameworks.
takeaways: AI literacy for non-specialists works best when embedded within broader digital literacy rather than taught in isolation — consider how to integrate AI concepts into existing capability-building programs.

Competency frameworks for AI should be 'holistic' (combining technical understanding, critical thinking, and ethical reasoning) rather than purely technical — design learning that addresses all three dimensions.
Middle school frameworks may provide scaffolding principles applicable to adult learners with limited technical background — review what progression models work for building foundational AI concepts.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears focused on public health faculty development context; findings may not generalise broadly to other sectors or disciplines without additional evidence on implementation scope.
takeaways: Faculty development programs can shift mindsets from AI resistance to readiness; consider designing similar change management approaches for your employee cohorts, starting with leadership buy-in and addressing underlying concerns.
Public health educators' transition strategies may include identifying and training 'AI champions' among staff who can model adoption and peer-mentor colleagues through literacy development.
Structured faculty upskilling likely requires balancing technical competency with domain-specific application — map this dual focus when designing AI literacy programs for your organisation.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience and surveys, likely skewed toward large enterprises and developed economies; specific recommendations may not apply uniformly across smaller organisations or less-resourced sectors.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will be most disrupted by gen AI, then prioritise upskilling pathways for those employees rather than attempting organisation-wide reskilling at once.

Design role-specific AI literacy programs that teach employees how gen AI affects their actual job tasks, not generic AI concepts — e.g. prompt engineering for writers, AI-assisted coding for developers.
Combine technical AI skills training with change management support to address employee anxieties about job displacement and build psychological safety around learning new tools.

articles.title: ASPIRE: a pedagogical framework for integrating generative artificial intelligence in public health education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: ASPIRE: a pedagogical framework for integrating generative artificial intelligence in public health education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — describes a pedagogical framework for public health education specifically; applicability to other sectors or disciplines unclear without seeing full methodology and evaluation results.
takeaways: Use structured pedagogical frameworks (like ASPIRE) when designing AI literacy programmes to ensure learning objectives are clearly mapped to AI competencies rather than adding AI tools ad hoc to existing curricula.
Design public health AI training to address domain-specific use cases (e.g. data analysis, diagnostic support, policy modelling) rather than generic AI literacy, to increase relevance and adoption.

Consider how generative AI changes teaching method itself — both as a subject to learn and as a tool educators use — requiring explicit discussion of AI limitations, bias, and governance alongside technical skills.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone; full article review needed to determine sample size, geographic scope, sectors studied, and methodological rigour.
takeaways: AI adoption in organizations has both positive and negative effects on employee creativity — understanding this dual mechanism is critical when designing implementation strategies to maximize creative output while mitigating productivity risks.

When rolling out AI tools, explicitly consider how task automation might reduce creative problem-solving opportunities for some roles, and design complementary upskilling or role redesign to preserve creative engagement.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited without access to full article — methodology, sample size, sector representation, and geographic scope are unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: AI-enabled transformation creates dual psychological pathways: capability and empowerment on one side, anxiety and job insecurity on the other — design interventions to strengthen the positive pathway while actively mitigating fear responses.

Corporate sustainability goals and AI adoption are interconnected through employee psychology — align your change communications to emphasise both organisational and employee benefits to shift the narrative from threat to opportunity.

Address job insecurity and anxiety directly during AI rollout; employees experiencing high job insecurity may disengage from capability-building efforts, creating a vicious cycle that undermines transformation outcomes.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methods — findings on psychological ownership and paternalistic leadership may be particularly relevant to Asian organisational contexts where this leadership style is more prevalent, limiting direct application to Western-style organisations typical in Australia.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customising or 'crafting' AI systems to fit their specific work needs — this sense of ownership can drive more collaborative human-AI working relationships.

Under paternalistic leadership styles, AI adoption may be enhanced by framing AI implementation as a leader-guided initiative that supports employee welfare and development, rather than a top-down replacement tool.

Employees who feel ownership over AI systems are more likely to actively collaborate with them rather than resist or underutilise them — consider design processes that give staff agency in shaping how AI tools work in their roles.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — reflects US labour market context and APA perspectives; may not fully capture uncertainty dynamics in other national employment systems, though broader psychological principles may apply.
takeaways: Organisational leaders should proactively communicate how AI adoption will affect roles and career paths to reduce worker anxiety and maintain psychological safety during technological transitions.

HR teams can implement structured uncertainty-reduction strategies (e.g. reskilling pathways, transparent timelines for AI implementation) to help employees build resilience and maintain engagement during organisational change.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and size, which are not described in the snippet. The mechanism (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) may apply broadly to knowledge workers, but geographic scope and sector diversity are unclear.
takeaways: AI adoption can harm employee mental health if not paired with strong psychological safety — ensure your change management strategy explicitly protects team members' ability to voice concerns, ask questions, and admit mistakes during AI implementation.

Ethical leadership is a protective factor during AI transitions — leaders should model transparent decision-making about AI use, acknowledge risks and limitations openly, and create forums where employees can discuss ethical concerns without fear of repercussion.

Monitor psychological safety metrics as a leading indicator during AI rollouts; declining safety scores may signal depression risk and warrant immediate intervention before mental health impacts accumulate.

articles.title: Worried about AI in the workplace? You’re not alone - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Worried about AI in the workplace? You’re not alone  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused survey data; findings reflect American worker concerns and may not directly transfer to Australian workplace contexts, which have different employment regulations, union presence, and cultural attitudes toward technology adoption.
takeaways: Worker anxiety about AI is widespread—use this as a starting point for psychological safety conversations rather than dismissing concerns as resistance to change.
Understanding the specific sources of worry (job security, skill obsolescence, fairness) helps tailor upskilling and change management interventions to address actual fears, not assumed ones.
Organizations can position themselves as trustworthy by being transparent about AI implementation plans and demonstrating commitment to employee wellbeing alongside technology adoption.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's consulting perspective reflects practices across their client base, but specific organisational context, industry sector, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Shift framing from 'AI adoption' to 'AI adaptation' — emphasise behavioural change and capability building rather than technology implementation alone to drive sustained engagement.

Design change interventions that explicitly target the human behaviours required for AI success, not just technical rollout; this may include reframing roles, decision-making processes, and skill expectations.
Use a structured change approach that moves beyond traditional adoption models to address mindset shifts and workplace norms that enable effective AI use.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on their consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample characteristics, methodologies, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Reframe AI adoption initiatives as workforce transformation projects requiring parallel changes to roles, skills, and organisational structure—not merely technology implementation.
Design behaviour change programmes that address employee concerns about automation and job security upfront, positioning AI as a tool that augments rather than replaces human capability.
Align learning and development pathways with the specific job transitions your organisation anticipates, rather than generic AI literacy training, to increase uptake and relevance.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and surveys, likely skewed toward large organisations in developed economies. Findings may not transfer directly to SMEs or resource-constrained sectors.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling not as a standalone training initiative but as part of broader organisational change management — this increases adoption and sustainability compared to isolated capability programs.

Embed change leadership practices (stakeholder engagement, clear communication of 'why', managing resistance) into your AI capability-building strategy to address the behavioural and cultural barriers that often derail technical upskilling.
Identify and equip change champions at multiple levels to model AI adoption and reinforce new ways of working, rather than relying solely on top-down mandates or one-time training events.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical sample or geographic scope. Insights may reflect US business school perspectives and may not generalise to Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation are most exposed to AI-driven change and prioritise upskilling conversations with those teams now, rather than waiting for disruption to occur.
Frame AI adoption as a behaviour change challenge requiring visible leadership commitment and clear communication about how roles are evolving, not just technology deployment.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings depend on the study's sample composition — the snippet does not indicate geographic scope, sector, or sample size. Moderate caution warranted until full methodology is reviewed.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical mediator between AI adoption and employee wellbeing; leaders should actively foster safe spaces for expressing concerns about AI tools before and during rollout to mitigate depression risk.

Ethical leadership practices during AI implementation directly buffer negative mental health outcomes; establish clear ethical guidelines and model them visibly to shape how employees perceive and adapt to AI changes.
Monitor and screen for depressive symptoms in teams undergoing rapid AI adoption, particularly in groups with lower baseline psychological safety — early intervention may prevent escalation.

articles.title: Agentic AI, explained - MIT Sloan
articles.snippet: Agentic AI, explained  MIT Sloan
articles.generalisability: Limited — provides conceptual explanation of agentic AI without empirical evidence or organisational case studies. Applicable conceptually across contexts but lacks evidence of effectiveness in specific workplace settings.
takeaways: Understand the distinction between reactive AI (responding to prompts) and agentic AI (independently planning and executing tasks) to identify where autonomous AI systems could reduce manual coordination overhead in your team.

Before adopting agentic AI tools, establish clear guardrails and monitoring systems, as autonomous agents require different governance frameworks than traditional AI assistants to manage unintended behaviours.

Map existing bottlenecks in your workflows where AI could act independently on defined objectives, starting with lower-risk tasks to build confidence in autonomous systems before scaling to mission-critical processes.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on broad psychological research on friendship and health outcomes across diverse populations, though specific studies cited may vary in geographic scope.
takeaways: Strong friendships have measurable physiological benefits — people with close social bonds show lower stress hormones, better immune function, and even longer lifespans than isolated individuals.
The 'friendship paradox' is real: most people underestimate how much their friends value them, meaning many of us are healthier and more liked than we realise.
Quality matters far more than quantity — a handful of genuine, reciprocal friendships deliver greater health benefits than a large network of superficial connections.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely moderate to high — appears to be a multi-country analysis of personality and music preferences, though specific sample details are unclear from the snippet.
takeaways: People's taste in music reveals consistent personality patterns across different countries and cultures — suggesting our musical choices tap into something universal about human temperament.
The finding challenges the idea that musical preference is purely cultural; personality traits seem to shape what we enjoy listening to regardless of where we live.
This quirky connection between personality and playlists hints that you could probably guess someone's broad personality type by eavesdropping on their music taste.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from snippet alone, but likely synthesises psychological research on true crime interest across populations; generalisability depends on breadth of studies reviewed.
takeaways: True crime's appeal taps into fundamental psychological drives — curiosity about danger, the need to understand threats, and the safety of experiencing risk from a distance.

People are drawn to true crime partly because it satisfies our desire to solve puzzles and feel intellectually engaged, which explains why the genre keeps audiences hooked despite (or because of) its dark subject matter.

Our fascination reveals something paradoxical about human nature: we're simultaneously repelled by and attracted to real human suffering, suggesting our brains use true crime as a low-stakes way to rehearse coping with danger.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews existing research on MBTI's predictive validity, but findings are limited by the mixed quality and scope of underlying studies on leadership outcomes.
takeaways: Despite MBTI's massive popularity in corporate settings, research shows it's surprisingly weak at predicting actual leadership behaviors — so those expensive team assessments might not tell you who'll be an effective leader.
The test's appeal lies in its simplicity and reassuring personality categories, not scientific accuracy — it's more entertaining than evidence-based for identifying leadership potential.

If you've been sorted into a 'natural leader' type, the finding might be humbling: your 4-letter code probably matters far less than your experience, skills, and how people actually respond to you in real situations.

articles.title: How dogs think - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How dogs think  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — snippet provides insufficient detail to assess scope, methodology, or generalisability of the underlying research.
takeaways: Dogs likely process information differently than humans — exploring canine cognition reveals surprising gaps between what we assume about their thinking and what they actually do.

Understanding dog cognition has practical implications for training and behavior, but also satisfies curiosity about whether our interpretations of dog behavior are accurate or projections of human logic.

articles.title: Personality traits linked to differences in brain structure - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Personality traits linked to differences in brain structure  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone, but neuroimaging findings typically have moderate generalisability — individual brain structure varies considerably, and correlations between personality and neuroanatomy are often small to medium effect sizes.
takeaways: Your personality might literally be written into your brain's physical structure — certain traits correlate with measurable differences in brain regions, suggesting personality isn't just psychology but neurobiology.
The finding highlights how interconnected mind and brain are: what we call 'personality' has a tangible neural basis, which is fascinating for understanding why people are fundamentally different.
This bridges the 'nature vs. nurture' gap — brain structure differences could explain personality consistency, or personality-driven behaviour could shape the brain over time.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The model linking AI adoption → psychological safety → depression suggests findings may apply across sectors, but geographic scope, sample size, and industry representation are unclear from information provided.
takeaways: AI adoption without deliberate attention to psychological safety can increase employee depression risk — leaders must actively create conditions where staff feel safe voicing concerns about AI implementation, not just roll out technology.

Ethical leadership is protective: managers who model and communicate clear ethical principles around AI use may buffer negative psychological effects, suggesting training should emphasise leader accountability for how AI is deployed, not just technical competence.
Monitor psychological safety metrics (employee voice, error reporting, willingness to challenge decisions) during and after AI adoption as early indicators of employee wellbeing risk.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG reports typically draw on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample details, methodology, and geographic scope are unclear from the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that invite all employees to contribute ideas and questions without fear of embarrassment or retribution — this removes barriers for underrepresented groups and improves decision quality.
Measure psychological safety regularly through anonymous surveys and act visibly on feedback; employees notice when leaders respond to concerns, which reinforces the safety culture.

Train leaders to model vulnerability, ask genuine questions, and reward dissenting views — manager behaviour is the primary lever for shifting psychological safety, especially in hierarchical or performance-driven organisations.

articles.title: How AI anxiety and contextual factors shape employee deviant innovation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How AI anxiety and contextual factors shape employee deviant innovation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. Findings on AI anxiety and innovation may apply across sectors, but geographic scope and sample diversity are unclear.
takeaways: AI anxiety can be a double-edged sword for innovation — monitor whether employee anxiety is driving risky, poorly-considered 'deviant' initiatives versus constructive challenge to status quo; psychological safety frameworks should distinguish between these.

Contextual factors (team norms, leadership support, organisational culture) appear to mediate how AI anxiety translates into behaviour — invest in transparent communication about AI strategy and role changes to reduce anxiety-driven unproductive responses.

Assess your team's current AI anxiety levels and psychological safety climate; employees under high anxiety may innovate in ways that undermine rather than strengthen organisational goals without clear guardrails and psychological support.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings on workplace psychological safety trends. Generalisability to Australian workplaces may be limited due to differences in employment law, workplace culture, and organisational practices between the US and Australia.
takeaways: Identify which dimensions of psychological safety (speaking up, risk-taking, help-seeking) are weakest in your team and design targeted interventions to address gaps rather than treating psychological safety as a single construct.

Use the APA's 2024 data on how workplace changes (remote work, restructuring, AI adoption) affect psychological safety to audit your own organisation's transition practices and anticipate where trust may erode.
Map psychological safety metrics against your retention and engagement data to quantify the business case for safety initiatives locally, rather than relying solely on US-based benchmarks.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis draws on global case studies and client work, but specific implementation details and industry applicability may vary; findings most relevant to large organisations with resources for AI transformation.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as expanding employee agency and decision-making power rather than automation-driven job replacement; this framing reduces anxiety and builds psychological safety around AI tools.

Design AI implementation with clear role clarity and decision rights — specify which decisions humans own, which AI informs, and which are delegated; ambiguity about AI's role undermines trust and safe adoption.

Create structured feedback loops where employees can flag AI failures or unexpected outputs without fear of blame; this surfaces real-world problems early and demonstrates that psychological safety extends to AI-related concerns.

articles.title: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety - Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.snippet: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety  Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual clarifications on psychological safety from a US-based academic institution, but lacks empirical data or specific organisational context. Applicability to Australian workplaces depends on whether misconceptions are similar across contexts.
takeaways: Identify which common misconceptions about psychological safety exist in your own organisation (e.g., confusing it with 'anything goes' culture or low accountability) and address them explicitly with leadership to prevent misaligned implementation.

Use clarified definitions of psychological safety to design targeted interventions — ensure stakeholders understand it requires both permission to speak up AND clear accountability, not permissiveness.
